text: Every Business Rule script works with two objects: current and previous. Current you've already been using. Previous is less familiar, and used correctly, it's how you detect exactly what changed in a save, not just that a save happened at all.

Current is a genuine GlideRecord, pointed at the exact record this Business Rule is processing. Everything you already know about reading and writing GlideRecord fields with dot notation applies directly. Inside a before rule, changes you make to current are folded into the save automatically — no extra call needed.

Previous is also a GlideRecord, but it represents the record's state before this update — a pre-update snapshot. It's only populated on update operations, and only when the rule's Advanced checkbox is turned on. On an insert, there's no before state to compare to, so previous simply doesn't apply.

The single most common use of previous is this comparison: checking whether a field on current differs from the same field on previous. That tells you specifically what changed. Here, the script detects a genuine escalation to priority one, and queues a notification to the assigned user's manager.

Notice the second condition: previous priority not equal to one. Without it, this logic would fire on every single save of a record that was already priority one, not just the moment it escalated. Current alone can never tell you that difference, because current only ever shows you the new value.

Current for the live state, previous for what changed from. Next, we'll look at the mistakes that pattern is meant to prevent — infinite loops, missing operation checks, and the other real, well-documented ways Business Rules go wrong in production.
